headline: Meta releases V2 of its non-invasive BCI that turns thoughts into keypresses
summary: Meta's Brain2Qwerty BCI uses magnetoencephalography (MEG) to read brain activity, avoiding surgery. The second version boasts significantly increased accuracy, reaching up to 78% word accuracy for some users.
details: Meta has released the second version of its non-invasive Brain2Qwerty brain-computer interface (BCI). This system allows users to control computers using their minds without requiring surgical implants, unlike solutions like Neuralink.

Brain2Qwerty uses a magnetoencephalography (MEG) scanner to detect faint changes in the brain's magnetic fields, correlating these signals to keypresses on a virtual keyboard. This approach bypasses the need for invasive procedures.

The latest version shows significant accuracy improvements, trained on ten times more data per test subject. It now achieves an average word accuracy of 61%, with the best participant reaching up to 78% accuracy, a substantial jump from the previous version's 40% average.

Despite these advancements, Meta acknowledges that 61% average accuracy is not yet sufficient for clinical testing or everyday conversation. Another challenge is the large size of current MEG sensors, which are much bigger than the user.

However, Meta is continuously improving the system with more training data and anticipates future advancements in MEG sensor technology will lead to smaller, more manageable devices. This development is a crucial step in neuroprosthetics, potentially restoring or improving quality of life for patients without surgery.
